**Surah 1: al-Fatihah**

Meccan, and its number of verses is seven.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

It is also called **Umm al-Qur'an** (the Mother of the Qur'an), because it is its opening and beginning, so it is like its root and origin. For this reason it is also called **Asas** (the Foundation). Or it is so called because it includes the praise of Allah, exalted is He, the worship of Him through His command and prohibition, and the explanation of His promise and warning. Or because it includes all its meanings, such as the theoretical wisdoms and the practical rulings, which are the following of the straight path and the knowledge of the ranks of the blessed and the stations of the wretched. It is also called **Surat al-Kanz** (the Treasure), **al-Wafiyah** (the Complete) and **al-Kafiyah** (the Sufficient), for this reason. It is called **Surat al-Hamd** (the Surah of Praise), **al-Shukr** (Gratitude) and **al-Du'a'** (Supplication), and **Ta'lim al-Mas'alah** (the Teaching of the Request), because it contains these. It is called **al-Salah** (the Prayer), because its recitation is obligatory or recommended in it. It is called **al-Shafiyah** (the Healing) and **al-Shifa'** (the Cure), because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is a cure for every disease." It is called **al-Sab' al-Mathani** (the Seven Oft-Repeated), because it has seven verses by consensus. However, some counted the basmalah but not ﴿أنعمت عليهم﴾ (the verse "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour"), and others reversed this. It is repeated in the prayer. Or it is called so because of its revelation, if it is authentically reported that it was revealed in Mecca when the prayer was prescribed, and in Medina when the qiblah was changed. It is authentically reported that it is Meccan, due to the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾ [al-Hijr 15:87], and this is Meccan by explicit text.

﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾

﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is part of al-Fatihah and of every surah. On this view is the recitation of the people of Mecca and Kufa, their jurists, Ibn al-Mubarak (may Allah have mercy on him), and al-Shafi'i. The reciters of Medina, Basra and Syria and their jurists, Malik and al-Awza'i, disagreed with them. Abu Hanifah (may Allah have mercy on him) did not state a clear ruling on it, so it was assumed that it is not part of the surah according to him.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan was asked about it and said: "What is between the two covers is the speech of Allah, exalted is He." We have many hadiths. Among them is what Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Opening of the Book is seven verses, the first of which is ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾." And the saying of Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her): "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited al-Fatihah and counted ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ and ﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ as one verse." Because of these two reports it has been disputed whether the basmalah is a verse on its own or together with what follows it. The consensus is that what is between the two covers is the speech of Allah, exalted is He, and there is agreement on its being written in the codices of the Qur'an, with great care in keeping the Qur'an pure, to the extent that "Amin" was not written.

The letter *ba'* (in *bismi*) is connected to an omitted element whose estimated form is: *bismi Allah aqra'* ("In the name of Allah I recite"), because what follows it is something that is recited. Likewise, every doer is understood to have something that makes the naming a beginning for it. That is better than estimating *abda'* ("I begin"), because there is nothing matching it or indicating it. Or *ibtida'i* ("my beginning"), because of the extra implication in it. Placing the object first here is more fitting, as in the saying: ﴿In the name of Allah is its sailing and its anchoring﴾ [Hud 11:41] and the saying: ﴿You alone do we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah 1:5], because it is more important, more indicative of exclusivity, more suited to glorifying, and more in harmony with existence. The name of Allah, exalted is He, is prior to the recitation. How could it not be, when He has made it the instrument of the recitation? An action is not complete, nor is it regarded as valid under the law, unless it is begun with His name, due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every important matter which does not begin with the name of Allah is cut off [lacking blessing]."

It was also said that the *ba'* is for accompaniment, and the meaning is: "Recite, seeking blessing by the name of Allah, exalted is He." This and what follows it until the end of the surah is spoken by the tongues of the servants, so that they may know how to seek blessing by His name, praise Him for His blessings, and ask from His bounty. The *ba'* was given a kasrah, though single letters should normally have a fathah, because it is specific to being attached and to the genitive case, just as the lam of command was given a kasrah, and the lam of possession enters upon the apparent noun. This is to distinguish between them and the lam of inception.

The word *ism* (name), according to our Basran scholars, is one of the nouns whose endings were dropped because of frequent use, and whose beginnings were made to have sukun (stillness). A hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza) was added to it at the start, because their habit is to begin with a moving letter and to stop on a still one. This is supported by its inflections: *asma'*, *asami*, *suma*, *sammaytu*, and the coming of *sumā* like *hudā* as a dialect form of it. A poet said:

"Allah named you a blessed name (*sumā*), by which Allah has preferred you with preference."

Metathesis (switching of letters) is a distant and irregular view. Its derivation is from *sumuww* (height), because it is elevation for the named and its emblem. Some Kufan scholars say it is from *simah* (mark). Its original form is *wasm*; the *waw* was dropped and the connecting hamza was put in its place, so that its alteration would be minimal. This was refuted on the basis that the hamza has not been known to enter upon a word whose initial letter has been dropped in their speech. Among its dialect forms are *sim* and *sum*. A poet said:

"In the name of the One whose mark is in every surah."

If by *ism* is meant the utterance, then it is other than the named, because it consists of separate sounds that do not remain, and it differs according to nations and eras, sometimes multiplying and sometimes unifying. The named is not like this. If by it is meant the essence of the thing, then it is the named, but it is not famous in this sense. The saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾ [al-Rahman 55:78] and ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la 87:1] means the utterance. This is because, just as the essence and attributes of Allah, exalted is He, must be exalted above imperfections, so too the words set for them must be exalted above obscenity and bad manners. Or *ism* here is an added (redundant) element, as in the poet's saying:

"Until the year's end, then peace be upon you both."

If by *ism* is meant the attribute, as is the view of Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, then according to him it is divided into what is the very named, what is other than it, and what is neither it nor other than it.

He said "*bismi Allah*" and did not say "*billah*" (by Allah), because seeking blessing and help is by mentioning His name. Or to distinguish between an oath (*yamin*) and seeking blessing (*tayammun*). The *alif* was not written, according to the normal practice of the script, because of frequent use, and the *ba'* was lengthened in its place.

**Allah**: its origin is *Ilah*. The hamza was dropped and the *alif-lam* was put in its place. For this reason it is said *Ya Allah* with a cut hamza (in the vocative). However, it is specific to the one worthy of worship in truth. *Ilah* in origin applies to any object of worship, but then it came to be dominant for the one worthy of worship in truth.

Its derivation is from *aliha, ilahatan, uluhatan, uluhiyyatan*, meaning "he worshipped." From this come *ta'alluha* and *istal'aha*. It was also said it is from *alaha*, meaning "he was bewildered," because minds are bewildered in knowing Him. Or from *alihtu ila fulan*, meaning "I found rest in him," because hearts are at peace in remembering Him, and spirits rest in knowing Him. Or from *aliha*, meaning "he was alarmed at a matter that befell him," and *alahahu ghayruhu* means "he gave him refuge," since the one seeking refuge runs to Him and He gives refuge, in reality or in his own assumption. Or from *alihai al-fasil*, meaning "the young camel became attached to its mother," since servants become attached to supplicating Him in hardships. Or from *walaha*, meaning "he was bewildered and his mind was confused." Its original form is *wilah*, and the *waw* was changed into a hamza because the kasrah on it is heavy, as the dammah is heavy, in several ways. So it became *ilah*, like *i'a* and *ishah*. This is refuted by its plural being *alihah* rather than *awlihah*. It was also said its origin is *lah*, the verbal noun of *lāha yaliyhu layhan wa lahan*, meaning "he hid himself and rose high," because He, exalted is He, is hidden from the perception of sights, and is high above everything and above what is not fitting for Him. The poet's saying supports this:

"Like an oath of Abu Rabah, in which his great *lah* (majesty) witnesses."

It was also said it is a proper name for His particular essence, because it is described and is not described by another, and because He must have a name by which His attributes are applied, and nothing else among what is applied to Him is suitable for that. Also because if it were a descriptive term, the statement *la ilaha illa Allah* ("there is no god but Allah") would not be a declaration of monotheism like *la ilaha illa al-Rahman* ("there is no god but the Most Gracious"), since the latter does not exclude partnership. The most evident view is that it is a descriptive term in its origin, but when it became so dominant that it is not used for anything else, and became for Him like a proper name, like *al-Thurayya* (the Pleiades) and *al-Sa'iq* (a name), it was treated like a proper name in the application of attributes to it, and in its not being described by another, and in there being no possibility of partnership being introduced to it. This is because His essence, considered in itself without any further consideration, is another real matter, or something else, which the human mind cannot grasp, so it cannot be indicated by a word. Also, if it indicated only His specific essence, the statement of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens﴾ [al-An'am 6:3] would not convey a correct meaning. Also, the meaning of derivation is that one of two words shares the meaning and structure of the other, and this is found between it and the aforementioned roots.

It was also said its origin is *Lāha* in Syriac, which was Arabized by dropping the final *alif*, adding the *lam* to it, and emphasizing its *lam* when what precedes it is fatha or dammah, as is the sunnah. It was also said it is emphasized in all cases. Dropping its *alif* is a solecism that invalidates the prayer and does not form a clear oath. It has come in poetry out of necessity:

"Behold, may Allah not bless Suhayl, when Allah has blessed the men."

**Al-Rahman al-Rahim** are two names formed for intensity from *rahima* (to show mercy), like *al-ghadban* from *ghadiba* (to be angry), and *al-'Alim* from *'alima* (to know). *Rahmah* in language means tenderness of the heart and a bending that calls for bestowing favour and kindness. From it comes *al-rahim* (the womb), because of its bending over what is in it. The names of Allah, exalted is He, are taken with regard to their ends, which are acts, not their beginnings, which are states of being affected.

**Al-Rahman** is more emphatic than **al-Rahim**, because the increase in the form indicates an increase in meaning, as in *qatta'a* and *qatha'a*, and *kubbar* and *kibar*. This is taken sometimes with regard to quantity and sometimes with regard to quality. On the first view it is said: "O Most Gracious of this world," because it encompasses both believer and unbeliever, and "O Most Merciful of the Hereafter," because it is specific to believers. On the second view it is said: "O Most Gracious of this world and the Hereafter," and "O Most Merciful of this world," because all the blessings of the Hereafter are great, while the blessings of this world are both great and small. Though analogy would call for progression from lower to higher, it is placed first because the mercy of this world comes first. Also, it has become like a proper name in that no other is described by it, because its meaning is the true Benefactor who has reached the furthest limit of mercy. This does not apply to anyone else, because whoever else is so is seeking recompense through His kindness and favour, desiring a great reward, a fine praise, or a mixture of natural tenderness, or love of wealth in the heart. Then He is, as it were, the intermediary in all of this, because the very existence of blessings, the power to deliver them, the motive that prompts this, the ability to benefit from them, and the faculties by which benefit is obtained, and everything else of His creation, none can have power over except Him. Or because *al-Rahman* indicates the great blessings and their roots, He mentioned *al-Rahim* to cover what goes out from them, so it is like a completion and an echo of it. Or it is for the sake of preserving the endings of the verses.

The more evident view is that it is not declinable (*ghayr munsarif*), even though its being specific to Allah, exalted is He, prevents it from having a feminine form of the pattern *fu'la* or *fa'lanah*, by analogy to what is most common in its category. He restricted the naming to these names so that the knower may know that what deserves to be sought help from in all matters is the true object of worship, who is the master of all blessings, both immediate and deferred, great and small. Then he turns with his whole being to the presence of holiness, holds to the rope of success, and occupies his inner self with remembering Him and preparing with Him instead of anything else.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 1, verse 2:

﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾. Al-hamd (praise, in the sense of commendation for a beautiful quality) is: the lauding of a beautiful, voluntary attribute, whether of a blessing or otherwise. Al-madh (laudation) is: the lauding of a beautiful quality without restriction. You say "I praised (hamidtu) Zayd for his knowledge and his generosity," and you do not say "I praised him (hamidtuhu) for his good looks," but rather "I lauded him" (madhtuhu). It has been said that the two are brothers. Al-shukr (gratitude) is: the requital of a blessing by word, deed and belief. He said:

"The blessings I have bestowed upon you have brought three things: my hand, my tongue, and the hidden conscience."

So shukr is more general than hamd in one respect and more specific in another. Since hamd is one branch of shukr, and is more widespread for the blessing and more indicative of its place (because belief is hidden), and given the possibility of the members of the body (in their conduct), hamd was made the head of gratitude and its principal element. Thus the prayer and peace of Allah be upon him said: "Praise is the head of gratitude, and whoever does not praise Allah has not thanked Him."

Dhamm (blame) is the opposite of hamd, and kufran (ingratitude) is the opposite of shukr. The word is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "lillah" (to Allah). Its original form is the accusative, and it has been read so. He departed from the accusative to the nominative in order to indicate the generality of praise and its permanence for Him, rather than its renewal and occurrence. It is among the verbal nouns (masadir) that are put in the accusative by hidden verbs, which are scarcely used alongside them. The definite article in it is for the genus, and its meaning is an indication to what everyone knows praise to be; or it is for totality (istighraq), since in reality all praise belongs to Him, for there is no good except that He is its bestower, either through an intermediary or without one, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾. In this there is an indication that He, exalted is He, is living, powerful, willing and knowing, since praise is not deserved except by one whose condition is this. It has been read "al-hamdu lillah" with the dal following the lam (i.e., al-hamdu lillahi with the lam vowelled to follow the dal), and vice versa, treating the two as they are used together as if they were a single word.

(p-28) ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. Rabb is originally a verbal noun meaning tarbiyah (nurture), which is bringing a thing to its completion gradually, step by step. Then it was applied as a description for the sake of emphasis, like sawm (fasting) and 'adl (justice). It has been said that it is an adjective from rabbahu, yurabbihi, so he is a rabb, as in your saying nammama, yanummu, so he is a numm (a tale-bearer). Then the owner was named by it, because he preserves what he owns and nurtures it. It is not applied to anyone other than Him, exalted is He, except in a qualified form, as in His saying: ﴿Return to your lord﴾. And al-'alam (world) is a noun for that by which something is known, like al-khatam (seal) and al-qalib (mould); it became predominant for that by which the Creator, exalted is He, is known, and it is every existent other than Him, of substances and accidents, for they, by their contingency and their need of an effecting, necessarily existent Being, point to His existence. He used the plural so that it would include the different kinds beneath it, and the rational beings among them became predominant, so it was pluralised with the ya' and nun, like their other attributes. It has been said: it is a term laid down for those possessed of knowledge, from the angels and the two weighty creatures (humans and jinn), and its application to others is by way of extension. It has been said: people are meant here, for each one of them is a world in that he comprises counterparts of what is in the greater world of substances and accidents, by which the Creator is known, just as He is known by what He originated in the greater world; for this reason he equated consideration of the two, and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And in yourselves; will you not see?﴾. It has been read "rabba al-'alamin" in the accusative, as a praise, or as a vocative, or by a verb implied by "al-hamd." In it is evidence that contingent beings, just as they need an originator at the moment of their origination, also need a sustainer at the moment of their continuance.

﴿Al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm﴾ (the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful): He repeated it for the purpose of giving a reason (ta'līl), for the reason we will mention.

﴿Māliki yawm al-dīn﴾ (Master of the Day of Judgement) is the reading of ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī and Yaʿqūb. Supporting it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when no soul will have power for another soul in anything, and the command that Day belongs to God.﴾ The rest read *Maliki* (malik). This is the preferred reading, because it is the reading of the people of the two sanctuaries (Ahl al-Ḥaramayn, i.e., Mecca and Medina), because of His saying: ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾, and because of the glorification it contains. *Mālik* is one who disposes freely of owned things as he wills, from *milk* (ownership). *Malik* is one who disposes by command and prohibition over those who are commanded, from *mulk* (sovereignty).

It has also been read *Maliki* with the light (takhfīf) pronunciation, and *Maleka* as a verb. *Mālikan* is read in the accusative, either as praise or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). *Mālikun* is read in the nominative, both nunated and annexed, as the predicate of an omitted subject. *Maliki* is read annexed in both the nominative and the accusative.

*Yawm al-dīn* is the day of recompense (jazāʾ). From this comes the saying, "As you judge (tadīn), so you will be judged (tudān)," and the verse from the *Ḥamāsa*:

"None remained but the aggressors; we repaid them as they had repaid."

The active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) is annexed to a time-expression, treating the time as if it were its object, by way of extension (ittisāʿ), like their saying: "O thief of the night (*yā sāriqa al-laylah*), the people of the house." Its meaning is: "He who possesses the affairs on the Day of Judgement," in the manner of His saying: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out﴾. Sovereignty belongs to this day in a continuous sense, so that the annexation is genuine, being prepared for the day's occurring as an attribute of a definite noun. It has been said that *al-dīn* means the Sharīʿa (law), and it has been said that it means obedience.

The meaning is "the Day of the recompense of religion." Singling out the day by the annexation is either to glorify it, or because God alone is unique in the enforcement of command on it. The bringing of these attributes to God, Exalted is He, namely that He is the Originator of the worlds, the Lord of them, the Bestower upon them of all blessings, outward and inward, immediate and deferred, the Owner of their affairs on the Day of Reward and Punishment, is to show that He is the one truly deserving of praise. No one is more deserving of it than He; indeed, in reality no one else deserves it. The placing of a ruling upon a description indicates that the description is its cause. By implication, whoever does not possess these attributes is not fit to be praised, let alone worshipped. Thus this serves as evidence for what follows.

The first attribute explains what makes praise obligatory, namely origination and nurturing. The second and third show that He bestows these favours by graciousness and free choice, and not because He is necessarily compelled to do so by His essence, nor because of an obligation upon Him arising from prior deeds, such that He would deserve praise on that account. The fourth establishes exclusivity, since it is something that admits no partnership in any way whatsoever. The passage also includes a promise to those who praise and a threat to those who turn away.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 1, verse 5:**

﴿You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help.﴾ Then, when the One deserving of praise was mentioned and described with great attributes that distinguish Him from all other beings, and knowledge became attached to a specific known object, He was addressed with this, as if to say: "O You whose state is this, we single You out for worship and for seeking help," so that the exclusivity would be more evident. This also serves the ascent from proof to direct vision, and the transition from absence (ghaybah) to presence (shuhud). It is as if the known object became something seen, the intelligible became something witnessed, and absence became presence. He built the beginning of the speech upon the initial state of the knower of God, which is remembrance, reflection, contemplation of His names, consideration of His blessings, and inference from His creation to the greatness of His affair and the dazzling brilliance of His dominion. Then He followed it with the final goal of that affair, which is that the servant plunges into the depths of arrival and becomes one of those who witness, seeing Him with his own eyes and conversing with Him face to face.

O Allah, make us among those who arrive by direct vision, not among those who merely hear reports.

It is a habit of the Arabs to vary their speech and to shift from one style to another, to refresh it and to stimulate the listener. Thus one shifts from address (khitab) to third person (ghaybah), and from third person to first person (takallum), and vice versa, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them...﴾ and His saying: ﴿It is Allah who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds, and We drive them...﴾, and the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Your night has stretched long with al-Ithmid,*
*and the one free of care has slept while you have not slept.*

*He passed the night, and a night was his too,*
*like the night of one with a sore eye, the sore-eyed one.*

*And that is news that came to me,*
*and I was informed of it by Abu al-Aswad.*

*Iyya* (إيّا) is a separate accusative pronoun, and the attached *ya'*, *kaf*, and *ha'* are particles added to indicate first person, second person, and third person respectively; they have no place in i'rab (grammatical inflection), like the *ta'* in *anta* (you) and the *kaf* in *ara'aytuka* (did you see you). Al-Khalil said: *iyya* is a noun prefixed to the pronoun suffix that follows it, and he argued with what he related from some Arabs: "When a man reaches sixty, then *iyyahu* (his) and *iyya al-shawabb* (the young ones)..." This is anomalous and not relied upon. It was also said that the pronouns themselves are the basis, and *iyya* is the support (*'umdah*), because when they are separated from the governing words, it becomes impossible to pronounce them alone, so *iyya* is added to them so that they can stand independently. It was also said that the pronoun is the whole combined form. It was read as *iyyaka* with an opened hamzah, and as *hayyaka* with the hamzah changed into a *ha'*.

*Ibadah* (worship, 'ibadah): the utmost extent of submission and humility. From it comes *tariq mu'abbad* (a paved road), meaning one that has been made smooth. And *thawb dhu 'abadah* (a garment with 'abadah) means one that is at the extreme of thickness. For this reason, it is used only for submission to Allah, Exalted is He.

*Isti'anah* (seeking help, isti'anah): asking for assistance. It is either necessary (darurriyyah) or not necessary (ghayr darurriyyah). The necessary help is that without which the act cannot be accomplished, such as the capability of the agent, his awareness of the act, the presence of an instrument and a material with which he acts upon it. When these are gathered, the man is described as capable, and it is valid for him to be charged with the act. The non-necessary help is the securing of what makes the act easy and smooth, like a mount for travel for one who is able to walk, or what brings the agent closer to the act and urges him toward it. This second kind is not a condition for the validity of the obligation. The intended meaning is asking for help in all matters, or in the performance of acts of worship. The hidden pronoun in the two verbs refers to the reciter and those with him among the guardian angels and those present at congregational prayer, or to him and all the monotheists. He includes his worship within their worship and mixes his need with their need, so that it may be accepted through their blessing and be answered. For this reason the congregational prayer was prescribed.

The object is placed first for glorification, for emphasis on it, and to indicate restriction. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Its meaning is: We worship You and we do not worship other than You." Also, what is prior in existence is placed first, and this serves as a reminder that the worshipper should direct his attention first and foremost to the One worshipped, and then to the worship, not insofar as it is an act of worship issuing from him, but insofar as it is a noble relation to Him and a lofty connection between him and the Real. For the knower of God only truly arrives when he becomes absorbed in contemplating the sacred presence and is oblivious to all else, to the extent that he does not contemplate himself or any of his states except insofar as they are contemplated by Him and attributed to Him. For this reason, what Allah related of His beloved (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) is superior when he said: ﴿Do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us﴾, over what He related of His interlocutor when he said: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾. He repeated the pronoun to make explicit that He alone is the One sought for help, and not anyone else. Worship was placed before seeking help so that the verse endings would correspond, and it is understood from this that placing the means before asking for the need is more likely to lead to acceptance.

I say: When the speaker attributed worship to himself, this might suggest boasting and self-admiration on his part regarding what issues from him, so He followed it with His saying: (p-30) ﴿and You alone do we ask for help﴾, to show that worship too is not completed or established for him except through help and success from Him. It was also said that the *waw* is for the state (*hal*), and the meaning is: "We worship You, seeking help through You." It was read with a kasrah on the *nun* in both verbs, and this is the dialect of the Banu Tamim, for they pronounce the present-tense prefixes with a kasrah except for the *ya'*, when the following letter is not pronounced with a dammah.

﴿Guide us to the straight path.﴾ This is an explanation of the help being requested, as if he had said: "How should I help you?" So they said, "(Guide us)." Or it is a specification of what is the greatest objective. Guidance (al-hidayah) is gentle indication (dalalah bi-lutf), and for this reason it is used in the sense of good. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ is an ironic usage (wārid ʿalā al-tahakkum). From the same root come al-hidayah, meaning the leading of wild animals to their preliminary paths (hawadi al-wahsh). The verb from it is hada, and its original construction is with the preposition lam or ila. It was treated as the construction of ikhtara (chose), as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And Moses chose his people﴾. The guidance of God, exalted is He, takes many kinds that cannot be counted, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you tried to count the favour of God, you could not number it﴾. However, it is confined to ordered categories:

The first: the bestowal of faculties by which a person is able to be guided to his interests, such as the intellectual power, the inner senses, and the outward perceptions.

The second: the setting up of distinguishing proofs between truth and falsehood, and between righteousness and corruption. To this He alluded when He said: ﴿And We showed him the two paths﴾, and He said: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness to guidance﴾.

The third: guidance through the sending of messengers and the sending down of books. By this He meant His saying: ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command﴾, and His saying: ﴿Indeed this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾.

The fourth: that He unveils the hidden things upon their hearts and shows them things as they really are, by revelation, or by inspiration and true dreams. This category is specific to the prophets and the saints (awliya'), and to it He alluded when He said: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾. And His saying: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾. Thus what is requested is either an increase in what they have been given of guidance, or steadfastness upon it, or the attainment of the ranks that are arranged upon it. So when the one who knows God and has arrived (al-ʿarif billah al-wasil) says it, he means: "Show us the way of travelling towards You, so that You may wipe away from us the darkness of our states, and remove the veils from our bodies, so that we may be illuminated by the light of Your holiness, and see You by Your light." Command and supplication share in wording and meaning, and differ by elevation and lowliness; and it is said that they differ by rank.

And al-sirat (the path): it is from sarata al-ta'am, when one swallows the food, as if it swallows the travellers (yasrutu al-sabilah). For this reason it was called luqam, because it engulfs them. And al-sirat comes from changing the sin into a sad, so that it matches the ta' in emphatic articulation (al-itbaq). The sad may be pronounced with a trace of the sound of the zay, so that it is closer to that which it replaces. Ibn Kathir, by the transmission of Qunbul from him, and Ruways from Ya'qub, recited it with the original sin; Hamza recited it with the intermediate sound (al-ishmam); and the rest recited it with the sad. The sad is the dialect of Quraysh. What is established in the Imam (the ʿUthmani codex) is the form with the sad. Its plural is surut, like kutub, and it is like al-tariq in masculine and feminine.

And al-mustaqim: the level, and what is meant by it is the path of truth. It is said that it is the religion of Islam.

﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ is a substitute (badal al-kull, a substitution of the whole) for the first, and it is in the position of repeating the governing verb, inasmuch as it is the intended referent in terms of the relation. Its purpose is emphasis and explicit specification, to establish that the path of the Muslims is the one witnessed to as upright in the most emphatic and eloquent manner, because it is made as an explanation and clarification of it. Thus it is as though it were among the self-evident matters, about which there is no obscurity, that the straight path is none other than the path of the believers. It has been said: "Those upon whom You have bestowed favour are the prophets." It has been said: "The Prophet ﷺ and his companions." It has been said: "The companions of Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, before distortion (tahrif) and abrogation (naskh)." It has been recited as: "The path of those whom You have favoured." *Inʿām* (bestowing favour) is the conveying of a blessing (niʿmah). Originally a blessing is the state that a person finds pleasant, and then the term is applied to what he finds pleasant of blessings, which is ease. The blessings of God, although they cannot be counted, as He says: ﴿And if you were to count the favour of God, you could not enumerate it﴾, are confined to two kinds: worldly and otherworldly.

The first (worldly) has two divisions: bestowed (mawhibi) and acquired (kasbi). The bestowed has two divisions: spiritual (rūḥānī), such as the breathing of the spirit into him and its illumination with reason and what follows from it of faculties such as understanding, thought and speech; and bodily (jismānī), such as the formation of the body, the faculties that inhere in it, and the conditions that accompany it of health and the perfection of the limbs. The acquired is the purification of the soul from vices and its adornment with noble character and virtuous dispositions, and the beautification of the body with innate forms and praiseworthy adornments, and the attainment of rank and wealth.

The second (otherworldly) is that He forgives him what he has neglected, is pleased with him, and settles him in the highest of the ʿIlliyyīn together with the honoured angels, for everlasting ages.

What is meant is the last division and what serves as a means to attaining it in the Hereafter, for what is other than that is shared by the believer and the unbeliever.

﴿Not of those who have incurred anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ is a substitute for (those) "those," in the sense that those bestowed upon are those who were safe from anger and error. Or it is a qualifying or specifying attribute of it, in the sense that they combined the absolute blessing, which is the blessing of faith, with safety from anger and error. This is valid only in one of two interpretations: treating the relative clause as an indefinite noun when it is not intended to refer to a known referent, as in the definite article in the poet's line:

"And indeed I pass by the base man who reviles me,"

and in their saying: "Indeed I pass by a man like you, and he honours me." Or it is treated as not definite by the annexation, because it is annexed to something that has one opposite, namely those upon whom favour has been bestowed, so the specification is fixed in the manner of movement without stillness.

It is reported from Ibn Kathir that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in the genitive, with the governing verb being "You have bestowed favour." Or by an implied "I mean." Or by exception, if "blessings" is interpreted as encompassing both categories. Anger (ghaḍab) is the stirring of the soul with the desire for retaliation; when it is ascribed to God, the intended meaning is the ultimate end and consequence, as already explained. "Upon them" is in the nominative position, because it is a substitute for the agent, unlike the first. The "not" (lā) is an added particle for emphasis of the negation implicit in "not (ghayr)," so it is as though he said: "Not those who have incurred anger, nor those who are astray." For this reason it is permissible to say "I, Zayd, not hitting," just as it is permissible to say "I, Zayd, not a hitter," although "I, Zayd, like a hitter" is not permissible. It has been recited as "and not the astray." Error (ḍalāl) is deviation from the straight path, deliberately or by mistake, and it has a wide scope, and the gradations between its lowest and highest degrees are many.

It has been said: "Those who have incurred anger" are the Jews, because of His saying concerning them: ﴿Whom God has cursed and upon whom He has become angry﴾. And "those who are astray" are the Christians, because of His saying: ﴿They have gone astray before, and have led many astray﴾. This has been transmitted as a prophetic report (marfūʿ). It may be said that "those who have incurred anger" are the disobedient, and "those who are astray" are those ignorant of God, because the one bestowed upon is the one granted success in combining knowledge of the truth for its own sake with good for acting upon it, and the opposite of that is the one in whom one of his two faculties, the rational and the practical, is defective. The one who fails in action is a wicked person upon whom anger falls, because of His saying concerning the one who kills deliberately: ﴿and God is angry with him﴾. The one who fails in reason is an ignorant, astray person, because of His saying: ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾.

It has been recited as "*al-ḍaʾlīn*" (with a hamza), in the dialect of those who strove to avoid the meeting of two unvocalised consonants.

**Āmīn** is a verbal noun (ism al-fiʿl, a noun functioning as a verb) meaning "answer" (istajib). 

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "I asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about its meaning, and he said: 'It is a word built on the vowel fatḥah, like *ayna*, because of the meeting of two unvocalised consonants.'"

Its alif is also found both lengthened and shortened. A poet said:

"May God have mercy on a servant who said *Āmīn*."

And he said:

"*Amīn*, so God increased between us the distance."

It is not from the Qur'an by consensus, but it is recommended to end the chapter with it, because of the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "Gabriel taught me *Āmīn* at the conclusion of my recitation of the Opening, and he said: 'It is like the seal upon a book.'" In its meaning is the saying of ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him: "Āmīn is the seal of the Lord of the worlds, by which He seals the supplication of His servant." The imam says it, and he says it aloud in the audibly recited prayers, because of what is related from Wāʾil ibn Ḥujr: "that he, upon him be blessings and peace, whenever he recited *wa-lā al-ḍāllīn*, said *Āmīn* and raised his voice with it."

It is reported from Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, that he does not say it. The well-known position from him is that he says it quietly, as related by ʿAbd Allah ibn Mughaffal and Anas. The follower prays *Āmīn* along with the imam, because of the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "When the imam says *wa-lā al-ḍāllīn*, then say *Āmīn*, for the angels say *Āmīn*, and whoever's *Āmīn* coincides with the *Āmīn* of the angels, his past sins will be forgiven."

It is reported from Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, that "the Messenger of God ﷺ said to Ubayy: 'Shall I inform you of a chapter the like of which has not been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, or the Qur'an?' He said: I said: Yes, O Messenger of God. He said: 'The Opening of the Book, it is the seven oft-repeated (al-sabʿ al-mathānī) and the Great Qur'an which I have been given.'"

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: "While the Messenger of God ﷺ was sitting, an angel came to him and said: 'Rejoice in two lights that you have been given, which no prophet before you was given: the Opening of the Book, and the final verses of the chapter of the Cow. You will not recite a letter from them except that you will be given it.'"

It is reported from Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Indeed, when God sends punishment upon a people as a decreed certainty, a child of their children reads in the Book: ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, and God hears it, and by that He lifts the punishment from them for forty years."
